edges.effect_quant: Exclusive breastfeeding shows a weak but fairly consistent protective association with childhood-onset type 1 diabetes, although the signal is sensitive to bias and exposure measurement.
edges.mechanism: Breastfeeding may delay exposure to foreign proteins, shape gut and immune development, and reduce inflammatory triggers during a period when autoimmune risk is being programmed. The biologic idea is plausible, but the epidemiology is noisy because feeding history is hard to measure accurately and often retrospective.
edges.summary: The boring claim is the right one here: breastfeeding may modestly lower later type 1 diabetes risk, particularly when exclusive breastfeeding lasts beyond the first weeks of life. The association survives pooled reanalysis, but it is not strong enough to treat as settled causal proof.
edges.caveats: Much of the evidence comes from observational studies with recall bias and heterogeneity in feeding definitions. Any protective effect is likely small, and it should not be overstated relative to genetic and other early-life drivers of type 1 diabetes.

evidence.citation: Cardwell CR et al 2012 Diabetes Care
evidence.notes: Breast-feeding and childhood-onset type 1 diabetes: a pooled analysis of individual participant data from 43 observational studies.

effect_quant.comparator: exclusive breastfeeding for more than 2 weeks versus shorter or none
